summaries.example: Imagine the sentence “Every blue marble is round.” Sherwood would ask what “every” does in the sentence. It helps us talk about all the things named by “blue marble.” He also studied words such as “is,” because “is” can connect a subject and a description in more than one way.
summaries.summary: William of Sherwood was a thirteenth-century English logician. He taught logic in Paris and wrote an Introduction to Logic and a work about special helper words in sentences. He wanted to explain how words stand for things, describe things, and affect reasoning. He studied statements about all members of a group, statements about one particular thing, and different meanings of words such as “is.” His lessons also included ways to remember the patterns of syllogisms, which are arguments made from connected statements. His work was important in medieval education and helped shape later discussions of logic and meaning.
key_ideas: William of Sherwood was an English teacher and logician of the 1200s who taught at the University of Paris.
His Introduction to Logic became one of the important logic textbooks of the thirteenth century.
He studied how words work inside sentences, especially words like “every” and “is.”
He treated some statements about one particular thing as an important kind of statement.
His ideas influenced later medieval thinkers, including Peter of Spain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sherwood shows that logic is not only about numbers or puzzles. It also asks how ordinary words guide our thinking. Questions about “all,” “some,” “is,” and “not” can change what a sentence means and what conclusions we may draw. Studying his work helps us see how people in the Middle Ages built tools for careful reasoning and how those tools influenced later teachers.

important_terms.definition: The study of careful reasoning: how statements fit together and what follows from them.
What a word helps us understand or point toward.
The job a word does in a sentence, such as standing for an object or describing it.
A word that needs other words to make its meaning work in a sentence, such as “every,” “if,” or “not.”
A kind of reasoning with two starting statements that support a conclusion.
A statement about all members of a group, such as “All birds are animals.”

questions_to_think_about: Why might a word such as “every” need special study?
How is “Socrates is running” different from “Socrates is not running”?
Can a sentence about something that does not exist still be useful?
Why would students want a short verse to remember rules of reasoning?

summaries.example: Consider “Every phoenix is an animal.” Sherwood distinguishes two readings of “is.” On one reading, the sentence is false if no phoenix exists, because it says something about actual beings. On another reading, it can function like a conditional: if something is a phoenix, then it is an animal. This analysis leads toward a distinction between actual things and merely possible things, although Sherwood’s account of modality does not simply match modern modal logic.
summaries.summary: William of Sherwood developed a distinctive thirteenth-century account of logic and semantics in the setting of Parisian terminist logic. His Introduction to Logic and Syncategoremata examine how expressions function within propositions and how those functions affect inference. Sherwood identifies four principal properties of terms: signification, supposition, copulation, and appellation. He gives special attention to supposition, including the unusual notion of manerial supposition and the semantic flexibility of singular terms. He also treats distributive expressions such as “every” as syncategorematic and analyzes “is” as ambiguous between actual and habitual being. This lets him give different readings of universal affirmative propositions and commit himself to a diminished mode of being for possibilia, things that could exist without existing. His logic also gives singular propositions a place alongside universal and particular forms, yielding a hexagonal pattern of relations, and supplies a mnemonic for syllogistic figures and moods. His account of modality distinguishes genuine modal constructions from merely categorical statements containing modal vocabulary, though the attributed works do not provide a treatment of modal syllogisms.
key_ideas: Sherwood’s two securely attributed works are an Introduction to Logic and the Syncategoremata, a treatise on syncategorematic terms.
His account of the properties of terms includes signification, supposition, copulation, and appellation; he gives supposition a central role in inference.
He recognizes singular terms, such as proper names and “this cat,” as capable of semantic variation, rather than leaving them outside the main theory.
He analyzes “every” as a syncategorematic term and argues that universal affirmatives require at least three appellata in the relevant discussion.
His treatment of “is” distinguishes actual being from a more conditional or habitual kind of being, producing different readings of universal affirmatives.
He explicitly incorporates singular statements into a hexagonal development of the traditional relations among categorical statements, and he is associated with an influential syllogistic mnemonic.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sherwood’s work illustrates how medieval logicians moved beyond commenting on Aristotle by developing detailed theories of language, reference, and inference. His distinctions show why small words can have large logical effects: changing the role of “is,” “every,” or “if” can change a proposition’s conditions and consequences. His treatment of singular terms and universal affirmatives also reveals that medieval logic was internally varied rather than a single unchanging system. important_terms.definition: A thirteenth-century approach to logic that studies both how terms function in sentences and how words such as “every” or “if” contribute meaning.
A presentation of something’s form to the understanding; Sherwood treats it as one basic property of terms.
The way a term stands for something in a sentence; Sherwood makes this the central property in his account.
The way an adjective, participle, or verb is ordered over or connected with something in a sentence.
The current, correct application of a term to things of which it can truly be predicated.
A word whose contribution depends on other meaningful words rather than standing for something by itself; examples include “every” and “if.”
An argument in which premises are arranged through a middle term to support a conclusion.
A statement-form concerning necessity, possibility, contingency, or impossibility; Sherwood also distinguishes broader and stricter uses of “mode.”

questions_to_think_about: Does “Every unicorn is an animal” have the same truth conditions if no unicorns exist? Which reading of “is” supports your answer?
Why might singular statements such as “Socrates is running” and “Socrates is not running” need a different relation from “Some people are running” and “Some people are not running”?
What is gained by treating “every” and “if” as meaningful sentence operators rather than as terms that stand for objects?
How can a mnemonic verse preserve logical information rather than merely helping students memorize names?
Should a historical theory be judged mainly by whether it resembles modern logic, or by the problems it was designed to solve?

summaries.example: Suppose a coach says, “Every player on this team is prepared.” The word “every” does more than name a group. It tells us to consider each player. Sherwood studied such words because they help organize the meaning of a whole sentence. He also distinguished “Socrates is running” from “Socrates is not running”: these disagree directly, rather than merely being two partly different claims.
summaries.summary: William of Sherwood was an English logician active in the thirteenth century. He taught in Paris during a period when scholars were developing new forms of logic alongside the study of Aristotle. His main works, an Introduction to Logic and the Syncategoremata, examine both arguments and the small words that shape sentence meaning. Sherwood describes four important properties of terms. Signification concerns what a word presents to understanding. Supposition concerns what a noun or pronoun stands for in a sentence. Copulation concerns how adjectives and verbs connect with what they say something about. Appellation concerns the things a term can presently be truly applied to. Sherwood also studies words such as “every,” which do not stand for objects by themselves but guide how other words work together. He treats singular statements as a distinct kind and develops relations among them, universal statements, and particular statements. His teaching includes a mnemonic for the forms of syllogisms. In discussing “is,” he distinguishes actual existence from a conditional or habitual reading. This creates an interesting question: a sentence about every member of a group may be understood differently depending on whether members of that group actually exist. His views on possibility and necessity were unusual for his time and were later rejected by some thinkers.
key_ideas: Sherwood was a thirteenth-century English logician connected with teaching at the University of Paris.
His Introduction to Logic was among the major logic textbooks of its century, and his Syncategoremata studied helper words in sentences.
He proposed four main properties of terms: signification, supposition, copulation, and appellation.
He gave special attention to singular terms and did not simply leave them out of theories about how terms stand for things.
He argued that “every” requires at least three things in the relevant class, because “all” is not normally used for only one or two.
His work included a memorable system for sorting syllogisms and influenced later medieval logicians, especially Peter of Spain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sherwood’s philosophy matters because it shows how careful reasoning depends on language. Words such as “every,” “if,” and “is” can change the scope or force of a claim, even though they may seem less important than nouns. His work also shows medieval scholars debating how statements refer to real, individual, and possible things. Learning about his distinctions helps students see that logic has a history: different thinkers proposed different systems for explaining meaning, truth, and valid inference. His ideas influenced other medieval logicians, even though later figures developed competing approaches.

important_terms.definition: A system for studying whether reasoning follows correctly from statements.
The way a word presents something to the mind or helps us understand what it is about.
The way a noun or pronoun stands for something within a sentence.
The way a describing word or verb connects with what it describes or says about.
The things that a term can correctly be said of at the present time.
A word whose meaning works together with other words in a sentence; “every” and “if” are examples.
An argument that uses two premises and a middle term to reach a conclusion.
A statement about one named or pointed-to thing, such as “Socrates is running.”

questions_to_think_about: Why might “every” work differently when there are two people than when there are many?
What does a name do in a sentence that an adjective or verb does not do?
How can the meaning of “is” affect whether a sentence is true?
Why would a logic teacher use a poem to remember syllogism patterns?
What might be the advantage of adding singular statements to a diagram of logical relationships?
